Read About Punta Cana

Columbus landed on this island in 1492 and called it the most beautiful place he had ever seen. What followed was five centuries of contested history — Spanish colonists, Haitian revolution, American occupation, dictatorship — and the eventual emergence of one of the world's most visited beach destinations from a coast that was essentially uninhabited jungle forty years ago.

Where the Americas began

On December 5, 1492, Columbus anchored in a bay on the northern coast of an island he named La Española — Hispaniola in its anglicized form. It was the first landfall in the Caribbean that would lead to permanent European settlement. Columbus established La Navidad that same December, a small fort built from the timbers of his wrecked flagship, making it the first European settlement in the Americas. The settlement was destroyed within a year, but the following year brought La Isabela, then Santo Domingo — founded in 1498 on the southern coast and still inhabited today, making it the oldest continuously occupied European city in the Western Hemisphere.

The Spanish proceeded to do what colonial powers do: mine, plant, enslave, and extract. The Taíno people who had lived on the island for centuries — a sophisticated culture that gave the world the hammock, the canoe, the barbecue, and the words hurricane and tobacco — were effectively wiped out within a generation, largely by smallpox but aided by forced labor. By 1520 the island's indigenous population had collapsed from an estimated half million to fewer than ten thousand. Their absence created the condition for what came next: the Atlantic slave trade.

Two countries, one island

Spain focused its colonial energy on the western end of Hispaniola, leaving the east — the future Dominican Republic — relatively underdeveloped. French settlers and buccaneers moved into the western third through the seventeenth century, and Spain formally ceded it to France in 1697. Saint-Domingue, as the French called it, became the most profitable colony in the Caribbean — and one of the most brutal. By the 1780s it was producing roughly forty percent of Europe's sugar and more than half its coffee, worked by enslaved people who outnumbered the colonists ten to one.

In 1791, those enslaved people revolted. The Haitian Revolution was the only successful slave revolution in history, and it produced the second independent nation in the Americas after the United States. Haiti declared independence in 1804. The Dominican Republic's path to independence was more complicated: it went through Haitian rule, Spanish reannexation, a brief second republic, and finally definitive independence in 1865. No other country in the Americas has had to declare independence three separate times.

Two nations, one island — divided by language, history, and a border that has never fully made sense geographically, but has defined everything politically.

The Dominican side ended up with roughly two-thirds of the island. The historical relationship between the two countries is fraught in ways that go back centuries and resurface regularly — in 2013 the Dominican Constitutional Tribunal stripped citizenship from people of Haitian descent, affecting hundreds of thousands of people and drawing international condemnation. The border is porous and contested. The history between the two nations is long, layered, and unresolved.

Trujillo and what came after

Rafael Trujillo governed the Dominican Republic from 1930 to 1961 and ran one of the most brutal dictatorships in the hemisphere. He renamed the capital after himself — Santo Domingo became Ciudad Trujillo — maintained files on hundreds of thousands of citizens, murdered political opponents abroad as well as at home, and in 1937 ordered the massacre of an estimated fifteen to twenty thousand Haitian migrants and Dominicans of Haitian descent along the border. It is known as the Parsley Massacre: soldiers allegedly used a person's ability to pronounce the Spanish word for parsley — perejil — to identify Haitians.

Trujillo was assassinated in 1961. The country cycled through democratic elections, a military coup, and a US military intervention in 1965 before arriving at a relatively stable if imperfect democracy in the 1970s. The CIA has been implicated in both the assassination of Trujillo and in subsequent interventions in Dominican politics. The country that tourists visit today — open, growing, largely peaceful — came out the far end of that history.

The beach that didn't exist

Punta Cana in the 1960s was a stretch of unpopulated coconut palms and beach on the eastern tip of the Dominican Republic. There was no road. There was no town. There were a handful of fishing families and not much else. The first visitors arrived by private plane — there was no other way — and stayed in a handful of bungalows. The developer was Frank Rainieri, a Dominican businessman, and his vision was simple: private beach, no noise, no crowds, all-inclusive.

The concept found its market. Punta Cana grew steadily through the 1970s and accelerated dramatically after 1984, when a proper international airport opened. The airport was initially owned and operated by a consortium of the founding hotels — the only privately owned commercial airport in the Americas — until 2006, when the government took a majority stake. Today it handles over eight million passengers a year and is the busiest airport in the Caribbean.

A strip of coconut-palm beach became the Caribbean's busiest tourist corridor inside a single generation — not because of history or culture, but because someone built an airport.

The all-inclusive model that defined Punta Cana was a deliberate choice, not an accident. The founders wanted to capture tourist spending on-property rather than having it leak into a local economy they couldn't control. It worked economically — for the resorts. The model keeps guests inside compound walls and minimizes contact with the wider country. Most visitors to Punta Cana have only the haziest sense of where they are in geographic or historical terms. This is partly what the product is designed to deliver: an absence of context, in exchange for unlimited buffet and a swim-up bar.

Merengue and its origins

The merengue is the national music of the Dominican Republic, and its origins are disputed in the way that origin stories often are when the culture in question was built by enslaved people who left few written records. What's clear is that by the mid-nineteenth century a fast, two-beat dance music was circulating in the Cibao valley in the north of the country, distinct from both the Cuban son and the Haitian kompa, played on accordion, güira (a metal scraper), and tambora drum. The combination is unmistakable: the güira's rasping shuffle under the accordion's rapid-fire melody, the tambora marking the beat underneath.

Trujillo adopted merengue as a political tool, promoting it as a unifying national symbol and having it played at official functions. He also demanded that merengue lyrics celebrate his regime, which they did, because musicians who refused faced consequences. The music survived his promotion of it largely by being better than any one person's agenda. After his death it absorbed new influences — jazz harmonies, salsa rhythms, electronic production — and spread through the Dominican diaspora in New York to become a globally recognized genre. Modern merengue is faster, more polished, and more international than the Cibao original. The güira is still in there, though.

The Taíno words you already know

Before Columbus, the Taíno had been living on Hispaniola for roughly a thousand years, having migrated north through the island chain from South America. They had a sophisticated agricultural system — growing yuca, sweet potato, maize, and pineapple — and a social structure organized around chiefs called caciques. Their ceremonial ball game, batey, was played on stone-lined courts and involved a rubber ball — rubber, from a tree they called caoutchouc — that predated the rubber industry by centuries.

The Taíno did not survive as a distinct culture, but their language permeated Spanish and English in ways that most speakers don't notice. Hurricane comes from huracán. Canoe from canoa. Tobacco from tabaco. Hammock from hamaca. Barbecue from barbacoa. Savanna from sabana. Maize, guava, papaya, iguana, manatee — all Taíno words. The people were effectively erased; the words survived because they named things that had no European equivalents, and those words are now so embedded in English that nobody thinks of them as indigenous borrowings.

What the all-inclusive conceals

The Dominican Republic is the largest economy in the Caribbean and Central America. It has grown rapidly over the past two decades, driven by tourism, remittances from the diaspora, and manufacturing in free-trade zones. By Caribbean standards it is large — the Hispaniola side of the island is roughly the size of Ireland — and genuinely diverse: beaches, mountains, desert, rainforest. The Pico Duarte, in the Cordillera Central, is the highest peak in the entire Caribbean at 3,098 meters. The country has whitewater rivers, coffee-growing highlands, and a colonial capital that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Almost none of this is visible from an all-inclusive resort in Punta Cana. The beaches there are genuinely extraordinary — a continuous arc of white sand and shallow turquoise water backed by palm groves, extending for miles — but they are also a highly managed experience designed to prevent the surrounding country from intruding. The resorts import staff, food, alcohol, and in some cases water. The arrangement works for visitors who want to decompress by the pool. It works less well for understanding where you are.

The country is worth knowing on its own terms. Santo Domingo's Zona Colonial has buildings that predate the Mayflower by a century. Altos de Chavón, a fabricated medieval Italian village above a river gorge an hour west of Punta Cana, has hosted Frank Sinatra, Julio Iglesias, and Metallica in a limestone amphitheater designed by Roberto Coppa. The Samaná peninsula in the north is a different climate zone, lush and less developed. The interior smells like coffee and cattle. The capital is loud and fast and intensely alive in ways that the beach corridor is deliberately not.
